summary: This document is a framing/significance text prepared for a VitaDAO/MIRA grant proposal, dated 12 November 2026. It argues the medical relevance of a centriole-age timing hypothesis by anchoring it to well-documented telomerase regulation in adaptive immune cells (T and B lymphocytes). The pilot experiment is conducted in fibroblasts (where centrioles can be tracked over months), with the broader therapeutic relevance grounded in immune senescence driven by persistent viral infection (e.g., CMV).

content_blocks.title: §1 — Why This Section Exists (MIRA Review Context)
content_blocks.content: The MIRA review scored therapeutic relevance 3/10 (or similar low score) and called the link between the assay and clinical relevance 'indirect.' The document acknowledges this criticism was valid against the previously submitted text, which argued from the assay rather than from the underlying biology. The revised paragraph (§3) is intended to fix this by grounding the claim in documented human biology without inflating any claim.

content_blocks.title: §2 — The In Vivo Anchor: Telomerase Regulation in Adaptive Immune Cells
content_blocks.content: The pilot experiment is run in fibroblasts because centrioles can be observed there for months. The medically relevant cell class is telomerase-positive, non-cancerous cells in vivo — specifically adaptive immune cells. The document presents a literature-supported sequence: (1) Resting lymphocytes have low telomerase activity; (2) Antigen-receptor stimulation sharply raises telomerase, enabling clonal expansion without immediate replicative loss; (3) Chronic activation leading to terminal differentiation causes telomerase activity to be lost again in CD8+CD28−CD27− T cells; (4) Persistent herpesvirus (CMV) driving continuous differentiation results in shorter telomeres in the circulating T cell pool vs. matched seronegative donors. The unresolved question is the TIMING — why a cell that can still induce telomerase stops doing so, and why lineages in the same milieu diverge in division rate. Centriole age is proposed as a candidate heritable timing mechanism.

content_blocks.title: Literature-Supported Sequence of Telomerase Regulation in Lymphocytes
content_blocks.content:
Step | What happens | Source
Resting lymphocyte | Low telomerase activity | Weng NP et al., J Exp Med 1996;183:2471 — PMID 8676067, DOI 10.1084/jem.183.6.2471
Antigen-receptor stimulation | Telomerase rises sharply; clone can expand without immediate replicative loss | Same (Weng 1996)
Chronic activation → terminal differentiation | Activity is lost again in CD8+CD28−CD27− T cells | Plunkett FJ et al., J Immunol 2007;178:7710 — PMID 17548608, DOI 10.4049/jimmunol.178.12.7710
Persistent herpesvirus (CMV) driving that differentiation | Shorter telomeres in circulating T cell pool than in matched seronegative donors | van de Berg PJ et al., J Immunol 2010;184:3414 — PMID 20176738, DOI 10.4049/jimmunol.0903442
B cells and general lymphocyte picture | Telomerase regulation across lymphocyte subsets | Weng NP, Springer Semin Immunopathol 2002 — DOI 10.1007/s00281-001-0093-4

content_blocks.title: §3 — Paste-In Paragraph (No Attribution) — Therapeutic Relevance Text
content_blocks.content: Ready-to-use paragraph for the proposal: Pilot runs in fibroblasts (centriole tracking over months). Medically relevant cell class: telomerase-positive, non-cancerous cells in vivo. Best-documented example: adaptive immune system. Resting T and B lymphocytes carry little telomerase; antigen-receptor signalling raises it sharply (Weng et al., J Exp Med 1996, PMID 8676067). Induction is not permanent: in highly differentiated CD8+CD28−CD27− T cells, activity is lost again (Plunkett et al., J Immunol 2007, PMID 17548608). CMV-seropositive donors have shorter telomeres in circulating T cell pool than matched seronegative donors (van de Berg et al., J Immunol 2010, PMID 20176738). The open question is timing — why a cell that can still induce telomerase stops doing so, and why lineages diverge in division rate (Mun et al., Immune Netw 2026, PMID 42405213). Inherited centriole age is a candidate mechanism for heritable timing asymmetry, testable only where single divisions can be followed for months. Explicitly states: 'None of this is my finding and none of it is a claim that the pilot will extend lifespan. It defines what the readout is for.'

content_blocks.title: §4 — Variant with Attribution (Aubrey de Grey Personal Communication)
content_blocks.content: Released for one-time use with date. Quote: 'rapidly dividing T and B cells during activation by persistent viruses such as CMV eventually stop reactivating telomerase, and there may be more going on that slows them down.' — Aubrey de Grey, personal communication, 12 Nov 2026. Permission covers: use in VitaDAO proposal, data-room documents, and review thread; one verbatim or trimmed quotation. NOT covered: claims of endorsement, his views on feasibility/bench risk/score, a second quotation, or his contacting VitaDAO on the project's behalf.

content_blocks.title: §5 — What This Section Does Not Do (Scope Limitations)
content_blocks.content: Explicit scope limitations: (1) Does not raise the therapeutic-relevance score by argument alone — only moves it if a reviewer concludes the question is worth a staged buy; described as 'the honest ceiling for a project with no data.' (2) Does not claim a target, a molecule, or an intervention. (3) Does not claim the pilot will show anything about T cells — the immune system is where the phenomenon is documented; fibroblasts are where the measurement is possible. This is a TRL 1 project by the document's own admission ('a project with no data').

content_blocks.title: Key References Cited
content_blocks.content:
1. Weng NP et al., J Exp Med 1996;183:2471 — PMID 8676067, DOI 10.1084/jem.183.6.2471 (telomerase in resting and stimulated lymphocytes)
2. Plunkett FJ et al., J Immunol 2007;178:7710 — PMID 17548608, DOI 10.4049/jimmunol.178.12.7710 (telomerase loss in CD8+CD28−CD27− T cells)
3. van de Berg PJ et al., J Immunol 2010;184:3414 — PMID 20176738, DOI 10.4049/jimmunol.0903442 (CMV and shorter telomeres in T cell pool)
4. Weng NP, Springer Semin Immunopathol 2002 — DOI 10.1007/s00281-001-0093-4 (telomerase regulation across lymphocyte subsets)
5. Mun S et al., Immune Netw 2026 — PMID 42405213, DOI 10.4110/in.2026.26.e27 (current review of T cell senescence; kinetics left open)

key_findings: Project is explicitly at TRL 1 — the document itself states 'the honest ceiling for a project with no data.'
MIRA review scored therapeutic relevance 3 (low) and called the link between assay and clinical relevance 'indirect'; this document is a remediation text.
Pilot experiment model system: fibroblasts, chosen because centrioles can be tracked for months — no immune cell experiments are described or planned in this document.
Proposed mechanism: inherited centriole age as a heritable timing mechanism for division-rate asymmetry in telomerase-positive non-cancerous cells (e.g., adaptive immune cells).

Medical anchor: well-documented telomerase regulation in adaptive immune cells — resting lymphocytes have low telomerase; antigen stimulation raises it; chronic activation (e.g., CMV) drives terminal differentiation and telomerase loss, resulting in shorter telomeres.

Open scientific question (the gap the project addresses): why cells that can still induce telomerase stop doing so, and why lineages in the same milieu diverge in division rate — current T cell senescence reviews leave the kinetics open (Mun et al., Immune Netw 2026, PMID 42405213).
No experimental data, no results, no quantitative readouts are presented in this document.
No target, molecule, or intervention is claimed.
Aubrey de Grey provided a personal communication (12 Nov 2026) supporting the framing but explicitly does not endorse the project or speak to bench feasibility.
The document is intended for use in a VitaDAO funding proposal and associated data-room materials.
